strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/a0849029004b4b0fb84f6cae28203dc3/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} develops a potentially valuable framework separating function-space functionals, permutation-invariant functionals, function-space operators, and permutation-equivariant operators.

The proposed expressive-equivalence result connects several prominent weight-space architectures through explicit simulations, offering useful conceptual unification beyond prior architecture-specific results.

The positive and negative results are paired thoughtfully: the paper identifies indistinguishable parameter configurations and explains how a general-position assumption can enable canonization and universality.

The manuscript is generally well organized, with clear motivation, informative diagrams, proof sketches in the main text, and extensive appendices. Its discussion of low-precision regimes and fixed output architectures identifies meaningful limitations and future directions.

The work is theoretical and does not require an empirical reproduction pipeline; definitions and intended constructions are documented in substantial detail. No material research-ethics concerns are apparent.
weaknesses: The central fixed-architecture impossibility result, Theorem F.9, is not established by the given proof. Its premise and equations (230), (250), and (251) evaluate f((x-a)/(b-a)) at x outside [a,b]^n, although f is defined only on X=[0,1]^n; this transformed argument generally lies outside X. The operator condition is therefore formally undefined. Moreover, the inference that a piecewise-affine region intersecting [a,b]^n forces affine equality at an exterior point needs a full-dimensional open intersection, which is not shown.

The growing-capacity universality theorem has a consequential statement/proof mismatch. Theorem F.10 claims the conclusion for any compact weight set K' that is a delta-approximator of K, whereas the proof explicitly requires K' subset V\E to invoke Lemma F.16 and Theorem 7.4. Arbitrary approximating sets can contain degenerate equal-bias configurations. The informal main-text theorem includes general position, but the formal result supporting the headline characterization does not.

Lemma F.15 contains another gap in the operator-universality chain: U_i is defined as a subset of K but is then asserted to cover the larger neighborhood B_{epsilon/4}(K). Consequently, the stated partition of unity on that neighborhood is not justified as written. This may be repairable by redefining the open sets, but the present proof is incomplete.

The canonization argument contains type and domain inconsistencies that obscure correctness. The canonization map returns an element of V^5, yet Lemma F.8 repeatedly applies Psi:V->V to cannon(v) and treats cannon(v) as an orbit representative in V; only its first feature channel has that property. Lemma F.6 also writes a permutation tuple including the output layer although the symmetry group excludes it. These may reflect omitted projections, but they occur in the main proof of equivariant universality.

The function-space-functional universality proof relies critically on a recent external separation-to-approximation theorem and asserts, without a sufficiently explicit argument, that the required separating DWS networks have a uniform architecture-dependent depth. The exact hypotheses of the invoked theorem and their satisfaction by the defined DWS class should be stated and verified for the result to be reliably reproducible.

There are additional correctness and presentation issues, including the input-dimension mismatch in Proposition E.7 (architecture input width one but the proof writes f_v(x,y)), inconsistent dimensions in Lemma F.7, and several claims of exact simulation after invoking approximation by MLPs. No experiments or sanity-check constructions are supplied to help validate the highly elaborate simulations.

The ideas are significant and plausibly original, but the unsupported function-space-operator results constitute one of the paper's four headline settings. Given these central proof deficiencies, the current evidence does not support the claimed comprehensive expressivity characterization; substantial technical revision is needed before acceptance.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/578bd6b82b084587904e010133abcf59/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} proposes a useful taxonomy separating function-space functionals, invariant weight-space functionals, function-space operators, and equivariant weight-space operators. This is conceptually clarifying and potentially significant.
The WL-based example distinguishing permutation orbits that message-passing architectures cannot separate is intuitive and helps expose limitations outside general position.
The paper is generally well organized, motivates the questions clearly, and supplies an extensive technical appendix.

The limitations section honestly identifies the absence of empirical validation, the restriction to MLP permutation symmetry, low-precision regimes, and the omission of optimization and generalization. I found no material research-ethics concern.
weaknesses: Soundness is the decisive problem. The fixed-architecture impossibility theorem (F.9) is not well posed: for x* outside [a,b]^n, Equation (230) evaluates f((x*-a)/(b-a)), generally outside f's declared domain X=[0,1]^n. Its proof also unjustifiably concludes that agreement with one affine piece on the inner cube forces agreement with the globally evaluated, piecewise-affine f at x*. Thus a headline result for function-space operators is unsupported.

The NFT results do not follow from the formal architecture. Definition D.12 includes LayerNorm and residual updates, but Proposition D.21 computes attention directly from raw scalar weights and later treats the feed-forward component as if it could replace features arbitrarily. With one scalar channel, LayerNorm removes precisely the information used in the proposed separation. Subsequent simulations likewise assume arbitrary feature padding, residual cancellation, and multi-head concatenation not supplied by the stated model. Moreover, the class labeled NFT_eq in Equation (48) ends with invariant cross-attention pooling into a vector, rather than an equivariant weight-space output. These inconsistencies undermine Proposition 5.3.

The neuron-identification construction underlying Theorems 6.3 and 7.4 is formally invalid as written. For W_l indexed by target i and source j, Equations (161), (162), and (174) attach b_{l-1,i} and b_{l,j}, reversing the required indices and sometimes referencing out-of-range entries when adjacent widths differ; one identifier is also left undefined. Although the intended correction may be apparent, this construction carries several central universality results and must be repaired and rechecked.

The growing-capacity theorem is inconsistent with its proof. Theorem F.10 quantifies over any compact delta-approximating K', whereas the proof requires K' to avoid the exclusion set. Existence of a general-position approximator is not established. Lemma F.15 also defines U_i as subsets of K while claiming they cover a neighborhood of K, and the final approximation adds a second error without allocating error budget. Consequently, the positive function-space-operator result is not proved as stated.

Several broad claims have incorrect or unclear quantifiers. Theorem E.4 asserts strict inclusions for an arbitrary weight space, while its strictness examples only cover particular ReLU architectures and the assertion is false for simple architectures. Related non-universality statements alternate between fixing V and existentially choosing a favorable architecture.

Reproducibility is poor for a theory paper because the principal results depend on malformed definitions, architecture mismatches, and proof gaps rather than merely omitted routine details. Important uses of recent separation-to-universality results also need their hypotheses—activation, bounded depth, and precise model class—checked explicitly.

The general-position results are qualitative and provide no approximation-size or conditioning bounds. Distinct biases may hold almost surely, but arbitrarily small bias gaps can make sorting-based constructions unstable or prohibitively complex. The paper presents these results as practical guidance without experiments or quantitative analysis; the limitations section acknowledges the lack of empirical validation, but this still substantially limits significance.

Overall, the taxonomy and intended theory are promising, but multiple central claims across architectural equivalence and function-space operators are presently unsupported. These are not isolated presentation issues and require major technical revision before the results can be relied upon.

strengths: Originality/significance: The four-way distinction among function-space functionals, permutation-invariant functionals, function-space operators, and permutation-equivariant operators is conceptually useful and organizes a fragmented literature into a coherent research agenda.
Significance: The claimed expressive equivalence among DWS, HNP/NP-NFN, GMN, and NG-GNN, together with the separate treatment of NFT, would be a meaningful unification if the proofs are corrected.

Soundness: The paper contains several convincing core ideas: functional separation via forward-pass simulation, a WL-based non-universality construction, and bias-based orbit canonization under a general-position assumption. It also appropriately identifies fixed output architecture as a potential bottleneck for function-space operators.

Presentation: The main paper is well motivated and readable, with effective overview figures, useful examples for each approximation setting, and extensive appendices containing definitions and proof attempts.

Reproducibility/limitations/ethics: The mathematical constructions are described in substantial detail, and the limitations section appropriately acknowledges the absence of empirical validation, optimization and generalization questions, low-precision degeneracies, and the restriction to MLP permutation symmetries. No material research-ethics concerns are apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central general-position universality proof contains dimensionally inconsistent neuron identifiers. With W_l in R^{d_l x d_{l-1}}, Eq. 161 assigns the row index i an identifier from layer l-1 and the column index j one from layer l; Eqs. 174, 224, and 225 repeat this reversal. These expressions can be undefined when adjacent widths differ, undermining Lemmas F.4-F.8 and thus Theorems 7.4 and 6.3 as written.

Soundness: The fixed-architecture negative theorem is not formally well-defined. In Theorem F.9, for x* outside [a,b]^n, the expression f((x*-a)/(b-a)) can evaluate f outside its declared domain X=[0,1]^n. Its proof also needs a more rigorous argument that every global linearity region intersects the inner cube with sufficient dimension to force the asserted affine continuation.

Soundness: The formal growing-capacity result, Theorem F.10, quantifies over any delta-approximating K' subset V, but its proof invokes Lemma F.16 and Theorem 7.4, which require K' subset V minus E. The GP condition appears in the informal main-text statement but is absent from the formal theorem, so the stated result does not follow.

Soundness/presentation: Several universality statements, including Theorems 6.3, 7.4, E.11, and F.2, say 'any' invariant/equivariant map without requiring continuity, although their proofs explicitly assume continuity and continuous networks cannot uniformly approximate arbitrary discontinuous targets. These are theorem-statement errors, not merely stylistic omissions.

Soundness: Lemma F.15 defines U_i as subsets of K but then claims they cover the larger neighborhood B_{epsilon/4}(K). The partition-of-unity construction therefore does not follow as written. This is probably repairable by redefining the sets, but it affects the proof of the positive function-operator theorem.

Reproducibility/evidence: The broad architectural-equivalence and function-operator claims receive no computational sanity checks, while some critical proof steps are deferred to cited universality results with conditions only briefly matched. Given the formal inconsistencies above, a careful proof audit and small numerical demonstrations would materially improve confidence.

Overall: The conceptual contribution is promising and potentially significant, but multiple errors touch the main universality and operator results. They appear plausibly repairable, yet the present manuscript is not sufficiently reliable for acceptance without substantial revision.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and underdeveloped question in weight-space learning and offers a useful four-way taxonomy separating function-space functionals, permutation-invariant functionals, function-space operators, and permutation-equivariant operators.

The expressive-equivalence analysis covering DWS, NFN variants, GMN, and NG-GNN is potentially significant. The manuscript gives explicit simulation arguments rather than relying only on informal architectural analogies, and it carefully identifies NFTs as a distinct case outside general position.

The general-position universality argument has a clear and insightful core: distinct neuron biases permit continuous orbit canonization, after which standard invariant/equivariant approximation machinery can be applied. The appendix also explores alternative exclusion sets and empirically measures how often the assumptions hold under quantization.

The proposed Output Capacity Expansion is simple, architecture-agnostic, and empirically effective. On the MNIST INR dilation benchmark, increasing the ensemble size improves both tested architectures monotonically, with GMN+OCE reducing reported MSE from 1.96 to 1.06 across three seeds.

The manuscript is generally well organized despite its technical density, includes extensive proofs and experimental details, discusses limitations without overstating ethical concerns, and reports compute, data splits, optimization settings, and uncertainty across seeds.
weaknesses: A central fixed-capacity limitation result, Theorem F.9, is not sound as written. It assumes f is defined only on X=[0,1]^n but evaluates f((x*-a)/(b-a)) for x* outside [a,b]^n, where the argument generally lies outside X. Thus Equation 231 and the theorem's hypotheses are undefined. The proof also asserts without adequate justification that every output linearity region must intersect the inner cube in a way that forces its affine rule to extend to x*. This theorem underpins a major part of the paper's claimed capacity characterization.

Several universality statements omit an essential continuity hypothesis. Theorems 6.3, 7.4, E.11, and F.2 state that 'any' invariant or equivariant map can be uniformly approximated, whereas their proofs explicitly assume continuity and continuous networks cannot uniformly approximate arbitrary discontinuous maps. Although surrounding definitions sometimes restrict attention to continuous functions, the formal theorem statements and approximation framework do not consistently enforce this condition.

The formal growing-capacity theorem is internally inconsistent with its proof: Theorem F.10 says the conclusion holds for any delta-approximating compact K', but the proof silently requires K' to lie outside the exclusion set. The main-text informal version includes this general-position restriction, while the formal appendix statement does not. Lemma F.15 also defines its purported cover U_i as subsets of K and then claims it covers a neighborhood of K, which is false as written. These gaps weaken confidence in the second central function-operator result.

The empirical method is only loosely connected to Theorem 7.2. That theorem enlarges the common input/output architecture and assumes input weights already belong to that sufficiently large architecture; OCE instead maps a small input network to an ensemble with a larger effective output representation. The conclusion itself acknowledges that mappings from smaller input networks to larger outputs remain future work, so the experiment should be presented as motivation rather than validation of the theorem.

The empirical evidence is limited to one transformation on one MNIST-INR dataset. There are no tests on the other claimed operator examples, other datasets, larger networks, or situations where output capacity is not expected to be the bottleneck. Comparisons to prior methods use numbers copied from different papers, while only the k=1 baselines are reproduced under the authors' setup, limiting the strength of the SOTA claim.

The claim that improvements occur with 'no additional parameters overall' is potentially misleading: trainable meta-network parameters are controlled by shrinking hidden widths, but OCE produces k times as many output weights and incurs substantially greater rendering memory and computation. Exact meta-network parameter counts, adjusted hidden widths, FLOPs, and inference costs are not reported.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript's code and log links are blank, and the appendix omits the precise DWS/GMN layer configurations and hidden widths used at each ensemble size. Consequently, the experiments cannot currently be reconstructed from the paper alone. The ethical discussion is acceptable for this primarily theoretical work, but the stated limitations should additionally acknowledge the proof restrictions and narrow empirical scope.

strengths: The four-way taxonomy—function-space functionals, invariant weight-space functionals, function-space operators, and equivariant weight-space operators—is clear and potentially useful for organizing future expressivity work.
The manuscript is generally readable and provides extensive appendices, explicit constructions, proof sketches, and an empirical examination of the general-position assumption.

The negative indistinguishability construction and the canonization-based approach under distinct hidden-layer biases are interesting ideas that could support valuable results after substantial correction.

Output Capacity Expansion is simple and improves both tested architectures monotonically as ensemble size increases; GMN+OCE reports an MSE of 1.06 versus the previous reported 1.60 result on the MNIST-INR dilation benchmark.

The impact statement is appropriate for this primarily theoretical work, and I see no unresolved ethical concern. weaknesses: Several central universality theorems are false as stated. Theorems 6.3, 7.4, E.11, and F.2 claim approximation of any invariant/equivariant map, without assuming continuity. Uniform limits of the continuous networks considered here cannot represent arbitrary discontinuous maps. The appendix proofs silently introduce continuity, so the claimed results and proofs do not match.

The fixed-architecture impossibility result is not well-defined. In Theorem F.9, f has domain X=[0,1]^n, while Equation (231) chooses x* outside [a,b]^n and evaluates f((x*-a)/(b-a)); that transformed point generally lies outside X. Thus a central premise, and consequently the proof, uses an undefined quantity.

Theorem F.10 also has a material statement–proof mismatch. Its statement quantifies over any compact delta-approximator K', but the proof additionally assumes K' is contained in V\E so that Theorem 7.4 applies. Nothing in Hausdorff approximation of realized functions guarantees this general-position condition.

Supporting arguments contain further gaps. Lemma F.15 defines U_i as subsets of K and then claims they cover a neighborhood B_{epsilon/4}(K), which they cannot. The proof of Theorem F.9 also makes an insufficiently justified inference from having M regions on a subcube to the structure and affine continuation of every region in a global PL_{M,R} representation.

The headline architectural-equivalence claim is overstated. The main text names ordinary NP-NFN among the equivalent prominent architectures, whereas Appendix D proves equivalence for NP-NFN+PE, a modified class supplied with unique input/output positional identifiers. The manuscript does not establish the advertised result for vanilla NP-NFN.

The practical evidence is much narrower than the claims suggest: only one MNIST-INR editing task, two base architectures, four ensemble sizes, and three seeds are evaluated. There are no tests on other function-space operators, larger architectures, non-INR applications, or settings directly exhibiting the proposed fixed-capacity obstruction.

The OCE comparison omits important costs and controls. Although the meta-network parameter count is said not to increase, OCE emits and evaluates up to eight output networks, increasing output storage and rendering/inference computation. Exact hidden widths, parameter counts, and compute per configuration are not reported, making the claimed isolation of output capacity difficult to verify.

The experiments do not validate the central theoretical mechanism. Monotonic gains from ensembling may reflect familiar ensemble effects; there is no comparison with an equally costly wider single output network or other enlarged output parameterizations, nor evidence that the target lies beyond the original architecture's representational closure.

Reproducibility is inadequate in the submitted artifact: both code references render as an empty “available at” location, and detailed model configurations are missing despite reported training costs of roughly 200 A100-GPU-hours. Several table baselines are imported from prior papers rather than rerun under fully documented matched conditions.

The limitations section acknowledges optimization/generalization and the simplicity of OCE, but omits the restrictive ReLU-specific negative result, dependence on general position, the single-benchmark evaluation, increased output inference cost, and the theorem-statement/proof discrepancies. Overall, the work has promising structure and ideas, but the unsupported central claims and reproducibility gaps prevent acceptance in its current form.

strengths: Originality/significance: The paper offers a useful unified framework separating four approximation settings—function-space functionals, invariant weight-space functionals, function-space operators, and equivariant weight-space operators. This taxonomy clarifies distinctions that prior work often leaves implicit.

The architectural-equivalence result covering DWS, HNP/NP-NFN, GMN, and NG-GNN, together with the qualified treatment of NFT, is potentially important: it consolidates several apparently different model families into one expressivity class.

The general-position analysis is conceptually strong. The paper states concrete exclusion sets, explains canonization through distinct biases or weight-row norms, and empirically checks how often these conditions hold for 60,000 trained MNIST INRs under quantization.

Presentation is generally clear and polished. The overview figures, theorem sketches, and extensive appendices make a technically dense contribution navigable; the rendered manuscript is visually clean.

The OCE modification is simple and practically useful. On the reported MNIST INR dilation benchmark, increasing ensemble size improves DWS from 2.29 to 1.36 and GMN from 1.96 to 1.06 MSE (×10^-2), under an approximately parameter-matched design.

The paper acknowledges meaningful scope limitations: it focuses on expressivity rather than optimization or generalization, primarily analyzes MLP weight spaces, and identifies low-precision regimes where its general-position assumptions become problematic. The impact discussion raises no apparent unresolved ethical issue.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central fixed-architecture limitation theorem (Theorem F.9, supporting Proposition 7.1 and the motivation for OCE) is not validly formulated. It takes f in C(X,Y) for X=[0,1]^n but evaluates f((x-a)/(b-a)) at x outside [a,b]^n; this transformed point generally lies outside X, where f is undefined. Interpreting f as a globally realized MLP would make the operator depend on a parameterization rather than only on the element of C(X,Y).

The proof of Theorem F.9 also makes an insufficiently justified leap: from having M regions on the inner cube and differing from a rescaled function at one exterior point, it concludes that the output cannot belong to the bounded-complexity class PL_{M,R}. The argument does not rigorously establish the required correspondence between global regions and the inner regions, yet this negative result is presented as a principal theoretical conclusion.

Theorem F.10 has inconsistent quantifiers and assumptions. Its formal statement says the conclusion holds for any compact delta-approximator K', whereas the proof explicitly requires K' to be contained in V excluding E. The informal main-text statement includes this general-position condition, but the formal appendix theorem omits it. Lemma F.15 also defines its proposed cover sets as subsets of K while claiming that they cover a neighborhood of K.

The main statements of Theorems 6.3 and 7.4 say “any” invariant/equivariant map, although uniform approximation by continuous networks requires the target to be continuous. The appendix proofs silently restore continuity. This is repairable wording, but important in a paper centered on precise universality characterizations.

The experimental evidence is narrow relative to the broad claim of practical relevance: OCE is evaluated only on one MNIST INR transformation, with two base architectures and three seeds. There is no test on another function-space operator, dataset, input-network capacity, or control comparing OCE against a single explicitly widened output network.

Reproducibility is inadequate in the submitted artifact. The code/configuration link is blank, and the appendix omits the actual DWS/GMN layer configurations and the parameter-matched hidden widths used for each ensemble size. Approximately 200 A100 GPU-hours are reported, but the supplied information is insufficient to recreate the models exactly.

The empirical comparison mixes newly trained OCE results with published baseline numbers. Although the authors state that the k=1 baselines were reproduced under their setup, fuller protocol matching and uncertainty-aware comparisons are needed, especially because GMN+OCE has a relatively large standard deviation (1.06 ± 0.13). Overall, the framework and ideas are promising, but flaws in a central limitation theorem and reproducibility gaps currently prevent reliable acceptance.
